opus-5.5.text:
Weather is a chaotic system, so small differences in the initial conditions grow over time. That's the butterfly effect people talk about. If you're uncertain about the state of the atmosphere over the Pacific today, that uncertainty propagates and amplifies. A week or two later it shapes what happens over North America or Europe. That creates a practical horizon for deterministic forecasting, generally put at around two weeks. Beyond it, the information from your initial measurement has been washed out by chaos.

The interesting part is that this limit isn't one fixed number. It depends on the scale and the phenomenon. Large-scale patterns like jet stream configurations or big pressure systems stay predictable longer than small-scale features like an individual thunderstorm. Some slowly evolving components also carry predictability further out: ocean temperatures, soil moisture, sea ice, phenomena like El Niño or the Madden-Julian Oscillation. So at subseasonal and seasonal timescales you can't say it will rain in this town on this day. You can still say something meaningful about the shift in the probabilities.

That's why I think the right framing is probabilistic. You don't want a single forecast trajectory. You want the full distribution of possible outcomes, and that's where ensembles come in. Traditionally, running large ensembles of numerical weather models has been very expensive. That's one place where AI models like FourCastNet change the picture. They're orders of magnitude faster, so you can run thousands of ensemble members. That lets you characterize the tails, the rare extreme events that matter most for things like heat waves or hurricanes.

The other piece is how well the models capture the actual physics of how influence travels. Disturbances propagate through things like Rossby waves, at certain speeds and along certain pathways. That's part of why we work with neural operators: you want to learn the underlying solution operator of the dynamics, consistent across resolutions, not just fit patterns on a fixed grid. The chaos sets a fundamental limit you can't beat. Within that limit there's a lot of room to do better, by being faster, more accurate, and better calibrated about uncertainty.

r001.rationale: It explains that small initial-condition differences amplify through chaos and calls this the butterfly effect, linking uncertainty over the Pacific to later weather elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It contrasts large-scale patterns and seasonal probability shifts with precise local rain forecasts, but never specifically distinguishes regional temperature averages from local weather uncertainty.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question that goes right to the heart of why weather is hard, and it's something we've thought about a lot in building FourCastNet.

The classical answer comes from Lorenz and the whole idea of chaos. The atmosphere is a nonlinear dynamical system, and small perturbations grow exponentially. So the famous "butterfly effect" is literally about this. A tiny change in Brazil can, in principle, influence a tornado in Texas, but the catch is that the influence is not a clean, traceable causal chain you can follow. The information propagates, but it also gets scrambled with everything else. So the question "how will weather here affect weather there" really becomes "how much predictability is there at all at that lead time and that spatial scale."

And the honest answer is that it depends enormously on scale. For large-scale features, like the position of the jet stream or a big blocking high, you have predictability out to maybe ten days, sometimes two weeks. For convective storms, for the precise location of a thunderstorm, it's hours. So the limit of predicting cross-location influence is really governed by the limit of predicting the intermediate dynamics that carry the information between those two places. You lose the small scales first, and then the error cascades upscale and eventually contaminates the large scales too. That's the upscale error growth that people like Lorenz and later Zhang and others formalized.

What's interesting from the machine learning perspective is that we're not trying to beat chaos. Nobody beats chaos. What we found with FourCastNet, and what the community has since found with GraphCast and Pangu and others, is that data-driven models can get close to the intrinsic predictability limit much more cheaply, and often with lower error than the numerical models at the same lead time. That's not because they've escaped the physics. It's because they're learning statistical structure in the data, including teleconnections, that numerical models capture only through resolving all the dynamics explicitly.

And that's where I think the real opportunity is. Things like El Niño's effect on North American winters, or the Madden-Julian Oscillation's influence on monsoon rainfall, those are the cross-location, cross-time relationships that matter for people. They're statistical, they're not deterministic, and they live at a scale where there is genuine predictability on seasonal timescales. So the right framing is probabilistic. You stop asking for a single trajectory and you ask for a distribution. That's why ensembles are so important, and why being able to run thousands of ensemble members cheaply with a neural model changes what questions you can even ask. You can actually estimate the spread, estimate the probability of an extreme, rather than running fifty expensive simulations and hoping they cover the tails.

The thing I'm most cautious about is extrapolation. A learned model is only as good as the climate it was trained on. If you ask how weather in one place affects another in a warming world, with regimes you've rarely or never seen, you really need the physics in the loop. That's why I keep coming back to hybrid approaches, neural operators that respect conservation laws and are constrained by the governing equations, so that when the data runs out, the physics carries you. The limit of predictability is a property of the system, but the limit of our models is something we can still push.

r001.rationale: The response invokes Lorenz’s chaos and the butterfly effect, explaining that small changes can influence distant weather while making the causal chain hard to trace.

r002.rationale: It contrasts predictability of large-scale features with the short predictability horizon for precise thunderstorms, but does not distinguish regional temperature averages from precise local weather.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between predicting a specific weather event and predicting how disturbances propagate. The atmosphere is a coupled system, so what happens in one region can influence another far away. But that influence isn’t a simple, fixed relationship—it depends on the state of the atmosphere in between and how that state evolves.

And because weather is chaotic, small uncertainties in our observations can grow over time. Even with a very good model, we don’t know the initial conditions perfectly. So there’s a limit to how far out we can make a precise prediction about a particular place.

That doesn’t mean we lose all predictive power beyond that point. We can run an ensemble of forecasts and ask which outcomes remain likely across different initial conditions. Some larger-scale patterns may be predictable even when the local details aren’t. So the question becomes: what are we trying to predict, over what timescale, and with what uncertainty?

r001.rationale: The response says weather is chaotic and small observation uncertainties grow over time, limiting precise forecasts—communicating the butterfly effect even without naming it.

r002.rationale: It contrasts potentially predictable larger-scale patterns with uncertain local details, but does not specifically distinguish regional temperature averages from precise local weather predictions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish between predicting the exact weather and predicting how a disturbance influences the system. The atmosphere is chaotic, so a small uncertainty in the initial conditions can grow over time. That puts a limit on how precisely we can say what will happen at a particular location on a particular day.

But that doesn’t mean there’s no predictability. Different processes operate at different spatial and temporal scales. A large-scale circulation pattern can carry information about how conditions in one region may affect another, even when the local details are uncertain.

So we should think in terms of ensembles and probabilities: if we perturb the starting conditions, which effects persist across those possible futures? And where do those futures diverge? The limit isn’t one universal cutoff. It depends on the phenomenon, the scale, and what you’re trying to predict.

r001.rationale: It attributes limits on precise predictions to chaotic growth of small initial-condition uncertainties, which conveys the butterfly effect.

r002.rationale: It contrasts large-scale circulation patterns with uncertain local details, but does not distinguish regional temperature averages from precise local weather predictions.
